title: Vicarious liability
subtitle: Whose fault is it, really? The two-stage test and its recent retreat
objectives: State the two-stage test for vicarious liability and explain precisely what each stage asks
Explain how 'akin to employment' extended stage 1 beyond the contract of employment, and identify the relationships capable of qualifying
Apply the current, narrowed stage-1 test to a novel fact pattern, recognising Barclays' retreat from an expansive reading

leadingAuthorities.citation: Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society [2012] UKSC 56
leadingAuthorities.role: Extends stage 1 beyond the contract of employment to relationships 'akin to employment'

leadingAuthorities.citation: Cox v Ministry of Justice [2016] UKSC 10
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms the akin-to-employment approach outside conventional commercial settings

leadingAuthorities.citation: WM Morrison Supermarkets v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 12
leadingAuthorities.role: Leading modern authority on stage 2, the close-connection test

leadingAuthorities.citation: Various Claimants v Barclays Bank plc [2020] UKSC 13
leadingAuthorities.role: Marks the retreat, tightening stage 1 back towards genuine integration

leadingAuthorities.citation: Trustees of the Barry Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses v BXB [2023] UKSC 15
leadingAuthorities.role: Applies the narrowed test; shows stage 1 and stage 2 can point in different directions

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can state 'employers are liable for their employees' torts' without hesitation. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the headline rule — this lesson is about the two-stage test hiding underneath it, and about a Supreme Court that has just pulled the test back in.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards application: expect fact patterns about care homes, franchises and volunteers, not bare definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and don't rush the two-stage structure — everything that follows, including the Barclays retreat, only makes sense once you can separate stage 1 from stage 2 without prompting.

overview.hook: A hospital doesn't perform surgery; a surgeon does. A children's home doesn't abuse a child; a member of staff does. Yet claimants routinely sue the institution, not the individual — and often win. Vicarious liability is the doctrine that lets a court hold one party responsible for another party's wrong without that party having done anything wrong itself. For decades the law asking 'when' kept getting wider. It has just started to narrow again.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 22 September 2026. Barclays and BXB are recent Supreme Court decisions; the boundary of 'akin to employment' remains an active area and further appellate clarification is plausible.

parts.heading: Two questions, not one
parts.voice: framing — lays out the architecture before any of the detail, so nothing that follows floats free
body: Vicarious liability is strict liability by proxy: the defendant is held liable for a tort it did not commit and could not have prevented, because of its relationship to the person who did commit it. That is a serious thing for the law to do, and it is why the courts have insisted, at least in theory, on a disciplined two-stage test before it bites.

Stage 1 asks a relationship question: is the wrongdoer in a relationship with the defendant that is either a contract of employment, or sufficiently 'akin to employment' to justify treating it the same way? Stage 2 asks a connection question, assuming stage 1 is satisfied: is the wrongful act itself so closely connected with that relationship that it is fair, just and reasonable to hold the defendant liable for it?

Students routinely blur the two stages into a single vague inquiry — 'was this person basically like an employee doing something basically work-related?' That vagueness is exactly what the Supreme Court has spent the last decade trying to discipline, first by expanding stage 1, then by reining it back in. Keep the two stages separate in your head from this point on; the rest of this lesson is organised around that separation.

components.definition: A strict, no-fault liability imposed on a defendant for a tort committed by another person, arising not from anything the defendant did but from the defendant's relationship to the wrongdoer — assessed through a two-stage test: (1) is the relationship akin to employment, and (2) is the wrongful act closely connected to it?

interaction.prompt: Vicarious liability requires the defendant institution itself to have been negligent or otherwise at fault.
options: False — it is a form of strict liability turning on relationship and connection, not on the defendant's own fault
True — the defendant must always have been careless in its own hiring or supervision
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. That is precisely what makes it doctrinally unusual, and precisely why the courts police the two-stage test so carefully — it is the only thing standing between a defendant and liability for someone else's wrong.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Careless hiring or supervision is a separate, fault-based claim in ordinary negligence. Vicarious liability is different: it can attach even to a defendant who did everything right in selecting and supervising the wrongdoer.

parts.heading: Stretching 'akin to employment'
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the institutional story before extracting the doctrine
body: For most of the twentieth century, stage 1 was simple: was the wrongdoer employed under a contract of employment? Independent contractors were outside vicarious liability altogether, however closely they worked with the defendant. Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society changed that.

The case concerned the sexual abuse of children at a residential school by members of the Institute of the Brothers of the Christian Schools — lay brothers bound by their religious vows, not employees of the school in any conventional sense. The Supreme Court nonetheless held the Institute vicariously liable, reasoning that the brothers' relationship with the Institute had all the features that make the employment relationship a fair basis for liability: it was akin to employment, even without a contract.

Lord Phillips set out the policy factors that justify vicarious liability wherever they are present — the defendant is more likely to have the means to compensate the victim and can insure against liability; the tort was committed as a result of activity undertaken on the defendant's behalf; the wrongdoer's activity is likely to be part of the defendant's business activity; the defendant created the risk by employing the wrongdoer; and the wrongdoer was, to a greater or lesser degree, under the defendant's control. Cox v Ministry of Justice confirmed the same approach applied even further from a conventional workplace: a prisoner working, unpaid, in a prison kitchen was held akin to an employee of the Ministry of Justice for these purposes, because her work was fully integrated into the prison's operations and undertaken for its benefit.

components.caseName: Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society
components.factsShort: Lay brothers of a Catholic religious institute, bound by vows rather than contracts, sexually abused children at a residential school they staffed.
components.ratioShort: A relationship without a contract of employment can still be 'akin to employment' for vicarious liability if it shares the relationship's defining features — integration into the defendant's activities, and undertaking that activity for the defendant's benefit.

expanded.facts: The Institute placed its brothers, under religious vows of obedience, to live and teach at a residential school managed by the Catholic Child Welfare Society. Brothers at the school committed systematic sexual abuse of pupils over many years. The claimants sought to hold the Institute vicariously liable, but the brothers had no contract of employment with anyone — their relationship with the Institute was governed by their vows.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Phillips held that the absence of a contract of employment was not decisive. What mattered was whether the relationship had the incidents that make it fair to impose vicarious liability: integration of the brothers' work into the operation of the school, the Institute's control over their assignment and conduct, and the fact that their activity was undertaken for the Institute's purposes and at its direction.
expanded.significance: This is the case that broke the contract-of-employment monopoly on stage 1. It opened the door to vicarious liability for religious orders, and — as Cox confirmed shortly after — for a wide range of other quasi-institutional relationships, from prisoners to volunteers, wherever the underlying features of integration and control are present.

components.label: The five Christian Brothers factors (stage 1)
points: The defendant is more likely to have the means to compensate the victim than the wrongdoer, and can be expected to have insured against liability
The tort will have been committed as a result of activity being undertaken by the wrongdoer on behalf of the defendant
The wrongdoer's activity is likely to be part of the business activity of the defendant
The defendant, by employing the wrongdoer to carry on the activity, will have created the risk of the tort committed by the wrongdoer
The wrongdoer will, to a greater or lesser degree, have been under the control of the defendant

interaction.prompt: Put these developments in stage 1 of vicarious liability in the order they occurred.
items: Stage 1 confined to relationships under a formal contract of employment
Catholic Child Welfare Society extends stage 1 to relationships 'akin to employment' without a contract
Cox confirms the akin-to-employment approach for a prisoner integrated into prison work
Barclays begins tightening stage 1 back towards genuine employment-like integration
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That is the arc of the doctrine: a strict contractual starting point, a decade of expansion through Christian Brothers and Cox, and then a deliberate correction in Barclays — which the rest of this lesson builds towards.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again. Stage 1 started narrow (contract only), was expanded by Christian Brothers and then Cox, and was only later narrowed by Barclays — the retreat came after the expansion, not before it.

parts.heading: Stage two: how close is close enough?
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the connection question as a live dilemma before resolving it with Morrison
body: Suppose stage 1 is satisfied — the wrongdoer's relationship with the defendant is akin to employment. Does that mean the defendant answers for anything the wrongdoer does, at any time, for any reason? Obviously not: an employee who commits an assault at a family party, wholly unconnected to their job, does not expose their employer to liability merely because they happen to be employed somewhere.

This is what stage 2 exists to police. The test, most authoritatively restated in WM Morrison Supermarkets v Various Claimants, asks whether the wrongful conduct is so closely connected with the acts the wrongdoer was authorised to do that it can fairly and properly be regarded as done while acting in the ordinary course of the relationship — even if the act itself was an unauthorised or even criminal mode of doing an authorised thing.

Morrison itself is instructive for showing the test's limits. An employee at the supermarket, Mr Skelton, had a grudge against his employer following a disciplinary process. He was given payroll data to transmit to an external auditor as part of his job — and instead copied it and, from home, on a weekend, deliberately leaked the personal data of thousands of colleagues online to harm Morrison. The Supreme Court held Morrison was not vicariously liable: Skelton's wrongful act was not closely connected to what he was authorised to do — it was an act of personal vendetta, using his access as opportunity rather than as the vehicle for a job-related task. Motive, the Court held, is a relevant consideration: an act done for purely personal reasons, disconnected from the employer's business, sits outside the field of activities entrusted to the wrongdoer even if the access that made it possible came from the job.

components.caseName: WM Morrison Supermarkets plc v Various Claimants
components.factsShort: A disgruntled payroll employee, entrusted with staff data for a legitimate audit task, deliberately leaked it online from home to harm his employer.
components.ratioShort: The close-connection test at stage 2 asks whether the wrongful act is so closely connected to the wrongdoer's authorised activities that it is fair to treat it as done in the ordinary course of the relationship; an act of purely personal vendetta, merely enabled by access from the job, fails that test.

expanded.facts: Morrison entrusted Skelton, a senior internal auditor, with the payroll data of around 100,000 employees so he could pass it to external auditors. Skelton, harbouring a grievance after being disciplined, copied the data onto a personal USB drive and later published it online and sent it anonymously to newspapers, seeking to damage Morrison.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Supreme Court held that although Skelton's role gave him the opportunity to access the data, the disclosure was an independent, personal criminal venture wholly unconnected to the task he had been asked to perform. It was not an unauthorised way of doing an authorised act; it was a different act altogether, motivated by revenge.
expanded.significance: Morrison confirms that close connection is not satisfied merely because employment provided the opportunity for wrongdoing. It reinforces that stage 2 is a genuine constraint, not a formality that follows automatically once stage 1 is met — a point the rest of this lesson returns to when Barclays narrows stage 1 itself.

components.definition: The stage-2 inquiry: whether the wrongdoer's tort is so closely connected with acts they were authorised to do that it is fair and just to treat it as done in the ordinary course of the employment-like relationship, even where the specific act was unauthorised or criminal.

interaction.prompt: Both scenarios involve an employee misusing data they had legitimate access to. In which is stage 2 (close connection) most likely satisfied?
interaction.scenarioA: A hospital records clerk, tasked with updating patient files, carelessly emails a file to the wrong recipient while doing that exact job.
interaction.scenarioB: A hospital records clerk, months after leaving a grudge unresolved, logs into the same system out of hours purely to leak a colleague's medical file to embarrass them personally.
interaction.explanation: A is a careless but authorised act done in the course of the very task the clerk was employed to perform — classic close connection. B mirrors Morrison: personal vendetta, using access as opportunity rather than doing the job badly, falls outside the field of activities entrusted to the employee.

parts.heading: Barclays: the retreat
parts.voice: argumentative — states the strongest case for continued expansion, then shows why the Supreme Court rejected it
body: By 2020, some lower courts and commentators had read Christian Brothers and Cox as pointing towards an ever-widening stage 1: almost any relationship involving some integration and some control might be 'akin to employment', particularly where the alternative left a vulnerable claimant without a solvent defendant to sue. On that logic, Various Claimants v Barclays Bank looked like a strong candidate for liability.

Dr Bates was a doctor engaged by Barclays, under a contract with the bank, to carry out pre-employment medical examinations of prospective employees at his own consulting rooms. He was not paid a retainer or salary; he billed a fee per examination; he held his own medical indemnity insurance; and he was free to, and did, carry out similar work for other clients. Decades later, claimants alleged he had sexually assaulted them during those examinations and sought to hold Barclays vicariously liable.

The Supreme Court held Barclays was not vicariously liable, because stage 1 was not satisfied: Dr Bates was, in the Court's words, 'in business on his own account' — a genuinely independent contractor, not someone in a relationship akin to employment. Lady Hale, giving the leading judgment, was explicit that the five Christian Brothers factors are not themselves the test for stage 1; they are policy reasons that explain why the employment relationship (and relationships akin to it) attract vicarious liability, deployed only once it is unclear whether a relationship is, or is closely akin to, employment. Where a genuine distinction between employment and business-on-one's-own-account can be drawn on ordinary principles, the inquiry stops there — the policy factors do not get a second, independent bite at extending liability.

This is the retreat this lesson's title promises. Barclays does not overrule Christian Brothers or Cox — both remain good law for relationships that really do share employment's defining features — but it corrects a drift towards treating 'akin to employment' as available wherever a claimant needs a solvent defendant. The test tightens back towards genuine integration and control, and away from mere involvement in someone else's institutional life.

components.title: Stage 1: how far the test has moved
components.description: A timeline showing the expansion and subsequent narrowing of the 'akin to employment' test at stage 1.

nodes.label: Pre-2012: stage 1 limited to a contract of employment; independent contractors excluded entirely
2012 — Catholic Child Welfare Society: relationships without a contract can be akin to employment if they share its defining features
2016 — Cox: akin-to-employment extended to a prisoner fully integrated into prison work, even unpaid
2020 — Barclays: retreat. The five policy factors are not themselves the test; a genuine independent contractor 'in business on his own account' falls outside stage 1
2023 — BXB: applies the narrowed test; confirms stage 1 and stage 2 are analytically separate and can point different ways

components.textAlternative: Stage 1 began strictly limited to contracts of employment. Catholic Child Welfare Society (2012) extended it to relationships akin to employment without a contract. Cox (2016) pushed this further, covering a prisoner integrated into prison work. Barclays (2020) then retreated, holding that the five policy factors are not an independent route to liability and that a genuine independent contractor in business on their own account falls outside stage 1. BXB (2023) applies this narrowed test and shows stage 1 and stage 2 can be answered differently on the same facts.

interaction.prompt: Where does Barclays sit on the expansion-to-retreat arc of the stage-1 test?
sliderLabels: Continues the expansion of Christian Brothers and Cox
Marks a deliberate retreat, tightening the test
interaction.explanation: Barclays does not abolish the akin-to-employment category, but it rejects treating the five policy factors as a freestanding route to liability and insists that a genuine independent contractor, in business on their own account, falls outside stage 1 — a clear tightening after a decade of expansion.

parts.heading: BXB: stage 1 and stage 2 can disagree
parts.voice: direct — sets up precisely the trap the test pool will probe
body: The Supreme Court's most recent word on this doctrine, BXB v Trustees of the Barry Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses, is worth ending on because it demonstrates something students consistently miss: satisfying stage 1 tells you nothing, by itself, about stage 2. The two questions are genuinely independent, and a case can fail on the second even after clearing the first.

Mark Sewell was a ministerial servant, later an elder, of the Barry Congregation. He befriended a young married couple, Mr and Mrs B, through his pastoral role, and used his position of trust and spiritual authority to groom and later rape Mrs B. The Supreme Court held, applying the narrowed Barclays approach, that Sewell's relationship with the congregation was capable of being akin to employment: elders were appointed by the congregation's structures, subject to its control and discipline, and their pastoral role was undertaken on the congregation's behalf and integrated into its activities. Stage 1 was satisfied.

But the claim still failed — on stage 2. The rape occurred at a private social gathering, at Sewell's home, in circumstances the Court found were not sufficiently connected to his formal role as an elder: the relationship of trust that made the abuse possible had grown through friendship and repeated pastoral contact over time, but the assault itself did not occur in the course of, or as a misuse of authority conferred by, any specific pastoral duty being performed at that moment. The close connection required at stage 2 was missing, even though the akin-to-employment relationship required at stage 1 was present.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that once a relationship is found to be akin to employment, vicarious liability more or less follows automatically — treating stage 1 as doing all the real work and stage 2 as a formality.
components.whyItsWrong: BXB shows precisely the opposite: stage 1 was satisfied, and the claim still failed, because stage 2 independently requires the wrongful act itself to be closely connected to the authorised activities of the role — not merely made possible by the trust or access that role conferred. Always run both stages, and never assume the second follows from the first.

interaction.prompt: In BXB, why did the vicarious liability claim ultimately fail despite the elder's relationship with the congregation being held akin to employment?
options: Because religious relationships can never satisfy stage 1
Because stage 2's close-connection requirement was not met — the assault was not sufficiently connected to duties being performed as an elder at the time
Because the congregation had no means to compensate the claimant
interaction.trapExplanation: The first option contradicts the case: stage 1 was satisfied, showing religious and pastoral relationships can be akin to employment post-Barclays where genuine integration and control are present. The claim failed at the independent, second hurdle — close connection — not at stage 1.

testPool.prompt: Name the two stages of the modern test for vicarious liability.
acceptableAnswers: akin to employment and close connection
testPool.modelAnswer: Stage 1 asks whether the relationship between the defendant and the wrongdoer is one of employment, or akin to employment. Stage 2 asks whether the wrongful act is sufficiently closely connected to that relationship to make it fair to hold the defendant liable.

testPool.prompt: Which case first extended stage 1 of vicarious liability beyond a formal contract of employment?
options: Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society
Various Claimants v Barclays Bank

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the five Christian Brothers policy factors relevant to stage 1?
options: The defendant is more likely to have means to compensate and to be insured
The wrongdoer's activity is likely to be part of the defendant's business activity
The wrongdoer personally profited financially from the specific tort committed
The defendant created the risk by employing the wrongdoer to carry on the activity
testPool.trapExplanation: Personal financial profit from the specific tort is not one of the five factors and is not the touchstone of the inquiry at all — the factors concern the structural relationship (control, integration, risk-creation, capacity to compensate), not the wrongdoer's motive or gain.

testPool.prompt: In Barclays, the Supreme Court held Dr Bates was NOT in a relationship akin to employment. What description did it use for his status?
options: 'In business on his own account'
'A quasi-employee of convenience'

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows when applying the modern two-stage test.
items: Identify the wrongdoer's relationship with the defendant
Ask whether that relationship is a contract of employment, or akin to it (stage 1)
If stage 1 is satisfied, ask whether the wrongful act is closely connected to the relationship (stage 2)
Impose vicarious liability only if both stages are satisfied

testPool.prompt: According to Barclays, what is the correct role of the five Christian Brothers policy factors in the stage-1 inquiry?
options: They are the test itself, to be applied afresh in every case regardless of the parties' formal relationship
They are policy reasons explaining why employment-like relationships attract liability, used only where it is unclear whether the relationship is genuinely akin to employment
They are irrelevant after Barclays and should be disregarded entirely
testPool.explanation: Barclays confirms the factors have not been abolished but demoted: they assist where the character of the relationship is genuinely unclear, but do not override a clear finding that the wrongdoer was an independent contractor in business on their own account.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below from Morrison, highlight the sentence that states the ratio on stage 2.
testPool.passage: The mere fact that the employment gave the employee the opportunity to commit the wrongful act is not sufficient to warrant the imposition of vicarious liability. What matters is whether there is a sufficient connection between the position in which the employee was employed and his wrongful conduct, such that it would be fair and just to hold the employer liable. Skelton's disclosure was an independent venture of his own, motivated by personal grievance, and was not so connected.
testPool.ratioSentence: What matters is whether there is a sufficient connection between the position in which the employee was employed and his wrongful conduct, such that it would be fair and just to hold the employer liable.

testPool.prompt: A cleaning company supplies a self-employed cleaner to a client's office under a contract that lets the cleaner set her own hours, use her own equipment, and refuse jobs, and requires her to carry her own public liability insurance. She damages a client's property through carelessness. Applying Barclays, is she likely in a relationship akin to employment with the cleaning company?
options: Yes — any relationship arranged through an intermediary company is automatically akin to employment
No — the features described (control over her own hours, own equipment, own insurance, ability to refuse work) point towards her being in business on her own account
Yes — because she is doing work that benefits the company's business
testPool.explanation: These are precisely the features Barclays treated as inconsistent with an employment-like relationship: autonomy over hours and methods, use of her own equipment, her own insurance, and freedom to decline work all point towards independent contractor status, not integration.

testPool.prompt: A charity places unpaid volunteers, fully under its direction and wearing its uniform, to supervise children on outings it organises and controls. A volunteer assaults a child during a supervised outing. Which stage-1 outcome is most consistent with Cox and Christian Brothers?
options: Stage 1 is satisfied — full integration, control and direction by the charity mirror the features that justified liability in Cox
Stage 1 automatically fails because volunteers are never employees
Stage 1 cannot be assessed because no money changed hands
testPool.explanation: Cox confirmed that unpaid, fully integrated work directed and controlled by the defendant can satisfy stage 1 — payment is not decisive. The volunteer here mirrors the prisoner in Cox far more than the independent doctor in Barclays.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario most closely mirrors the reasoning in Barclays, rather than Cox?
testPool.scenarioA: A self-employed IT consultant, invoicing per project, free to work for other clients and using his own equipment, is retained by a bank to fix a server and steals client data while doing so.
testPool.scenarioB: A prison inmate works unpaid in the prison laundry under full staff direction and control, and negligently injures a fellow inmate using laundry equipment.
testPool.explanation: A mirrors Barclays: an independent contractor, free to work elsewhere, using his own equipment and billing per project, is in business on his own account. B mirrors Cox: full integration and control by the institution, notwithstanding no payment, points towards a relationship akin to employment.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario most relevant to the stage-2 close-connection inquiry, assuming stage 1 is already satisfied.
testPool.scenarioText: A care home orderly, employed and fully integrated into the home's staff, is asked to help an elderly resident get dressed. During that task, he steals cash he notices in the resident's drawer.
tappableSpans: steals cash he notices in the resident's drawer
testPool.correctSpan: steals cash he notices in the resident's drawer
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right focus. Stage 1 is already settled by the facts (employed, integrated); the live question is whether the theft — occurring in the course of, and made possible by, the authorised dressing task — is closely enough connected to it, which is the stage-2 inquiry Morrison and BXB are both concerned with.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Stage 1 (employment, integration) is given in the facts and settled. The interesting question here is stage 2: whether the theft, occurring during and enabled by the authorised task, is closely connected to it.

testPool.prompt: A private tutoring agency places Ahmed, a self-employed tutor who sets his own rates and schedule and uses his own teaching materials, with a family for weekly one-to-one lessons at the family's home. Over several months Ahmed builds a relationship of trust with the family's teenage son and grooms him. Analyse whether the agency could be held vicariously liable, addressing both stages.
factsToOrder: Ahmed is self-employed, sets his own rates and schedule
Ahmed uses his own teaching materials
Ahmed builds trust with the son over several months of tutoring
The grooming occurs through contact enabled by the tutoring relationship

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the tutoring agency is vicariously liable for Ahmed's grooming of the son, applying the two-stage test.
modelAnswer.rule: Stage 1 asks whether Ahmed's relationship with the agency is akin to employment, applying Barclays' distinction between employment-like integration and being in business on one's own account. Stage 2, if stage 1 is satisfied, asks whether the wrongful conduct is closely connected to Ahmed's authorised activities (Morrison, BXB).
modelAnswer.application: On stage 1, Ahmed's self-employment, control over his own rates and schedule, and use of his own materials point strongly towards him being in business on his own account, much like Dr Bates in Barclays — the agency likely did not direct or control how he taught, only introduced him to the family. If stage 1 nonetheless failed for the agency, stage 2 would ask whether the grooming, built through the trust of the tutoring relationship over months, was closely connected to the tutoring itself; BXB shows that trust built through a role does not automatically satisfy close connection unless the wrongful conduct itself is sufficiently tied to duties being performed.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The claim is likely to fail at stage 1: Ahmed's independence, self-set terms and use of his own materials place him in business on his own account rather than in a relationship akin to employment with the agency.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures what BXB adds to the doctrine, beyond Barclays?
options: It confirms religious or pastoral relationships can never satisfy stage 1
It confirms stage 1 and stage 2 are analytically independent, so a relationship can be akin to employment yet the specific wrongful act still fail the close-connection test
It abolishes the close-connection test in favour of a single-stage inquiry
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option is contradicted by BXB's own finding on stage 1. The real contribution of BXB is procedural discipline: it shows the two stages can pull apart, with stage 1 satisfied and stage 2 failing on the same facts.

testPool.prompt: After Barclays, does satisfying one or more of the five Christian Brothers policy factors automatically establish stage 1?
options: No — the factors are an aid used where the character of the relationship is genuinely unclear, not an independent route to liability
Yes — satisfying any single factor is sufficient on its own

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating stage 1 and stage 2 as one blended question, or assuming that clearing stage 1 makes stage 2 a formality. BXB exists precisely to correct that: always run both stages, separately, on every fact pattern.
